Theorem: Let $p$ be any prime number. The set of $p$-adic numbers $\mathbb{Q}_p$ is an uncountable set.

Proof:
The set of $p$-adic numbers $\mathbb{Q}_p$ contains the set of $p$-adic integers $\mathbb{Z}_p$ as a subset. 
Every $p$-adic integer can be uniquely represented as a formal power series $\sum_{i=0}^\infty a_i p^i$, where each digit $a_i$ is an integer such that $0 \le a_i < p$.
Thus, there is a natural bijection between the set of $p$-adic integers $\mathbb{Z}_p$ and the set of all infinite sequences $(a_0, a_1, \ldots)$ with elements in $\{0, 1, \ldots, p-1\}$.
This set of all such infinite sequences is exactly the Cartesian product $\{0, 1, \ldots, p-1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$.
Since $p$ is a prime number, $p \ge 2$, meaning the set $\{0, 1, \ldots, p-1\}$ has at least 2 elements.
The Cartesian product of an infinite sequence of a set with at least 2 elements is uncountable; in particular, its cardinality is at least $2^{\aleph_0}$, the cardinality of the continuum.
Therefore, $\mathbb{Z}_p$ is uncountable.
Since an uncountable set cannot be a subset of a countable set, any set containing an uncountable subset must itself be uncountable.
Since $\mathbb{Z}_p \subseteq \mathbb{Q}_p$ and $\mathbb{Z}_p$ is uncountable, it follows that $\mathbb{Q}_p$ is uncountable.
$\blacksquare$
